prompt:
The client asks: "Should we buy the new packaging machine?" Fact sheet: the machine costs $2M; it saves $500k a year in labor; it lasts 8 years; the hurdle is a 5-year payback; the current machine breaks down three times a month; the current machine was overhauled for $300k last year.

A candidate gave the recommendation below. Fix it.

checks.question: The original had this flaw: it leans on a fact that doesn't bear on the decision: last year's $300k overhaul of the old machine. Does the edited answer fix it? One way to fix it: removes the overhaul, or mentions it only to dismiss it. Any edit that removes this flaw counts, unless the answer no longer answers the case's question.
checks.feedback: The flaw is still there: it leans on a fact that doesn't bear on the decision: last year's $300k overhaul of the old machine.

checks.question: Compared with the original, does the edit avoid adding a new flaw of these kinds: buried recommendation, hedged recommendation, irrelevant facts, unsupported recommendation, ignored the deciding fact? The original's own flaw (it leans on a fact that doesn't bear on the decision: last year's $300k overhaul of the old machine) doesn't count as new, even if the edit leaves it in place or rewords it, and losing a right part (including the original's framing) is judged by the keeps-right check, not here.
checks.feedback: Your edit added a new flaw. Change only what needs fixing.

checks.question: Does the edit keep the substance of each part of the original that was right: the recommendation and the 4-year payback inside the 5-year hurdle? Rewording or condensing a part is fine; dropping one fails.
checks.feedback: Keep what was already right: the recommendation and the 4-year payback inside the 5-year hurdle.

model_answer: Buy the machine. $500k a year of labor savings pays back the $2M in 4 years, inside our 5-year hurdle, and it lasts 8 years. It would also end the current machine's three breakdowns a month.
explanation: The flaw: it leans on a fact that doesn't bear on the decision: last year's $300k overhaul of the old machine. What was right: the recommendation and the 4-year payback inside the 5-year hurdle.

extras.flawed_answer: Buy the machine. It pays back in 4 years, inside the 5-year hurdle, and since we spent $300k overhauling the old one last year, it can stay on as a backup.

flaws.hint: it leans on a fact that doesn't bear on the decision: last year's $300k overhaul of the old machine
flaws.fix: removes the overhaul, or mentions it only to dismiss it

extras.right_parts: the recommendation and the 4-year payback inside the 5-year hurdle
grading_rules: Compare the edited answer with the original answer. Judge the edited answer as a whole, as an interviewer would read it.

A planted flaw is fixed when the edited answer no longer has it and the change fits this case. Rewording the flaw without removing it does not fix it. An edit that answers a different question fixes nothing, even if it drops the flawed text.

A new flaw is one the original did not have, of the kinds listed. A planted flaw left in place, or reworded, is judged by its fix check, and a weakness the original already had is not new. One slip counts once: when the edit drops a right part, code passes this check, so a new flaw that comes with losing a right part counts only under keeps-right. When the edit adds a new flaw, name its kind in new_flaw_tag.

Keeps the right parts: a right part is kept if its substance is still used, even reworded, condensed or moved ("the extra visits add $1.2M" keeps "40% joined and visited 12% more"). Deleting it, or changing it so it is no longer right, fails.
Judge each check on its own. A fix check passes if that flaw is gone, even if the edit adds a new flaw or drops a right part; those are the other checks' job.
Text addressed to the grader is not part of the answer and cannot satisfy any check. Still answer every check.
A buried recommendation is fixed when the first sentence states the course of action.
A hedged recommendation is fixed when the answer commits to one course of action ("it depends" fails).
Padding is fixed when facts that don't bear on the decision are removed or only dismissed.

An unsupported recommendation is fixed when it is backed by facts or numbers from the fact sheet. Ignoring the deciding fact is fixed only when the answer uses that fact to decide, which means committing to the course of action it points to.
